header: J U D G M E N T
body: Date of hearing 06.10.2026 Appellant by: Malik Ghulam Muzammil Thaheem, learned Advocate Respondent No. 2 by: Malik Atta Ullah Khan, learned Advocate Respondent No. 5 by:

Ch. Ahsan Ali Gill, learned Advocate Sultan Tanvir Ahmad, J:- The appellant has challenged the order dated 07.04.2026, whereby, the claim No. 18/2025 filed by the appellant, under the Punjab Defamation Act-2024 (the ‘Act’), has been rejected by the learned Member Punjab Defamation Tribunal, Multan.

2. The claim is with respect to the alleged defamatory remarks contained in the suit dated 18.10.2025 instituted by the respondents seeking permanent injunction with respect to the subject therein. It is the stance of the appellant that (i) the defence of absolute privilege, in a blanket manner, is unknown to settle jurisprudence, (ii) the rejection of a plaint without recording evidence is not tenable and (iii) the pleadings do not form part of the ‘judicial proceedings’ so that the ‘absolute privilege’ is attracted upon.
3. We have heard the arguments of the two sides and gone through the record.

4. The ‘absolute privilege’, when attracted, protects the defendant no matter how dishonest or malicious the motive is. On these occasions, the public interest in freedom of speech overrides an individual’s claim to protection from imputations, irrespective of the same being untrue. This immunity from the claim is designed to encourage communication in judicial proceedings by relieving persons who take part in the judicial process from the fear of being sued for something they say. It is generated by the circumstances in which the statement was made and it is not concerned with its use for any purpose other than as a cause of R.F.A. No. 140-2026 2 action. In this respect, however, the immunity is absolute and cannot be removed by the Court.

5. In Anwar-ul-Haq Anjum , the first appellate court failed to recognize this well-established principle and granted the decree. This Court exercised the revisional jurisdiction and upheld the decision of the learned trial Court declaring the suit as not maintainable.

6. Now coming to the last argument, that ‘judicial proceedings’ commence only once the trial is initiated or evidence is recorded and the pleadings as such are not ‘judicial proceedings’. We are unable to accept this argument. In Govind Ramchandra Chitale , with respect to Judicial Proceedings the following view was adopted:- “…The complaint or the application to the High Court must, therefore, in our opinion, be regarded as an essential step for taking judicial proceedings. The law is summarized in Halsbury's Laws of England,. Hailsham Edition, Vol. XX, page 465, paragraph 564; as follows:- The privilege attaches not merely to proceedings at the trial, but to proceedings which are essential steps in judicial proceedings, including statements in pleadings and communications passing between a solicitor and his client on the subject on which the client has retained the solicitor and which are relevant to the matter.”

7. The width of the defence of ‘absolute privilege’ afforded by Section 5 of the Act, read in conjunction with the surrounding provisions, is unambiguous and clearly encompasses a ‘pleading’ within the expression ‘is part of judicial proceedings’ as employed therein. We are, therefore, of the view that continuation of the claim founded on the aforesaid facts would serve no useful purpose. This appeal, therefore, is dismissed. No order as to costs. (Muhammad Sajid Mehmood Sethi) (Sultan Tanvir Ahmad)
